claim: Preterm infants that suffer cerebellar insults often develop motor disorders and cognitive difficulty.
source: Preterm infants that suffer cerebellar insults often develop motor disorders and cognitive difficulty.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that is supported by established clinical knowledge about preterm infants with cerebellar damage.

claim: Excitatory granule cells are the most numerous neuron type in the brain.
source: Excitatory granule cells, the most numerous neuron type in the brain, are especially vulnerable and likely instigate disease by impairing the function of their targets, the Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience literature about cerebellar granule cells.

claim: Excitatory granule cells are especially vulnerable to cerebellar insults.
source: Excitatory granule cells, the most numerous neuron type in the brain, are especially vulnerable and likely instigate disease by impairing the function of their targets, the Purkinje cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and knowledge about cerebellar development and vulnerability.

claim: Excitatory granule cells likely instigate disease by impairing the function of Purkinje cells.
source: Excitatory granule cells, the most numerous neuron type in the brain, are especially vulnerable and likely instigate disease by impairing the function of their targets, the Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the abstract that is tested in the study.

claim: Purkinje cells are the targets of excitatory granule cells.
source: Excitatory granule cells, the most numerous neuron type in the brain, are especially vulnerable and likely instigate disease by impairing the function of their targets, the Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar circuitry.

claim: Mutant mice lacking the majority of excitatory cerebellar neurons were generated using regional genetic manipulations.
source: Here, we use regional genetic manipulations and in vivo electrophysiology to test whether excitatory neurons establish the firing properties of Purkinje cells during postnatal mouse development. We generated mutant mice that lack the majority of excitatory cerebellar neurons and tracked the structural and functional consequences on Purkinje cells.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Purkinje cells fail to acquire their typical morphology in mutant mice lacking excitatory cerebellar neurons.
source: We reveal that Purkinje cells fail to acquire their typical morphology and connectivity, and that the concomitant transformation of Purkinje cell firing activity does not occur either.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Purkinje cells fail to acquire their typical connectivity in mutant mice lacking excitatory cerebellar neurons.
source: We reveal that Purkinje cells fail to acquire their typical morphology and connectivity, and that the concomitant transformation of Purkinje cell firing activity does not occur either.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The transformation of Purkinje cell firing activity does not occur in mutant mice lacking excitatory cerebellar neurons.
source: We reveal that Purkinje cells fail to acquire their typical morphology and connectivity, and that the concomitant transformation of Purkinje cell firing activity does not occur either.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by electrophysiological data.

claim: Mutant pups have impaired motor behaviors.
source: We also show that our mutant pups have impaired motor behaviors and vocal skills.
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments described in the study.

claim: Mutant pups have impaired vocal skills.
source: We also show that our mutant pups have impaired motor behaviors and vocal skills.
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral experiments described in the study.

claim: Excitatory cerebellar neurons define the maturation time-window for postnatal Purkinje cell functions.
source: These data argue that excitatory cerebellar neurons define the maturation time-window for postnatal Purkinje cell functions and refine cerebellar-dependent behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Excitatory cerebellar neurons refine cerebellar-dependent behaviors.
source: These data argue that excitatory cerebellar neurons define the maturation time-window for postnatal Purkinje cell functions and refine cerebellar-dependent behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Abnormal cerebellar development instigates motor diseases and neurodevelopmental disorders including ataxia, dystonia, tremor, and autism.
source: Abnormal cerebellar development instigates motor diseases and neurodevelopmental disorders including ataxia, dystonia, tremor, and autism.
evidence: This is supported by established clinical and scientific knowledge.

claim: Motor diseases and neurodevelopmental disorders have a high incidence in premature infants.
source: These conditions have a high incidence in premature infants as well as in newborns with cerebellar hemorrhage (Dijkshoorn et al., 2020; Limperopoulos et al., 2007; Steggerda et al., 2009; Zayek et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: Motor diseases and neurodevelopmental disorders have a high incidence in newborns with cerebellar hemorrhage.
source: These conditions have a high incidence in premature infants as well as in newborns with cerebellar hemorrhage (Dijkshoorn et al., 2020; Limperopoulos et al., 2007; Steggerda et al., 2009; Zayek et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: Affected children ultimately attain a smaller cerebellar size compared to children born full-term.
source: The affected children ultimately attain a smaller cerebellar size compared to children born full-term (Limperopoulos et al., 2005; Volpe, 2009), and they have altered functional connectivity between the cerebellum and the neocortex (Herzmann et al., 2019; Hortensius et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Premature infants have altered functional connectivity between the cerebellum and the neocortex.
source: The affected children ultimately attain a smaller cerebellar size compared to children born full-term (Limperopoulos et al., 2005; Volpe, 2009), and they have altered functional connectivity between the cerebellum and the neocortex (Herzmann et al., 2019; Hortensius et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: There is a strong correlation between abnormalities in cerebellar size and the subsequent incidence of cognitive disorders.
source: Observations from human clinical data indicate a strong correlation between abnormalities in cerebellar size and the subsequent incidence of cognitive disorders, suggesting that the late-term stage of cerebellar development encompasses a critical developmental time-window for establishing not only the motor but also the non-motor circuitry that is required for complex cerebellar functions and behavior (van der Heijden et al., 2021b; Volpe, 2009; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: The late-term stage of cerebellar development encompasses a critical developmental time-window for establishing motor circuitry.
source: Observations from human clinical data indicate a strong correlation between abnormalities in cerebellar size and the subsequent incidence of cognitive disorders, suggesting that the late-term stage of cerebellar development encompasses a critical developmental time-window for establishing not only the motor but also the non-motor circuitry that is required for complex cerebellar functions and behavior (van der Heijden et al., 2021b; Volpe, 2009; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from clinical observations and supported by citations.

claim: The late-term stage of cerebellar development encompasses a critical developmental time-window for establishing non-motor circuitry.
source: Observations from human clinical data indicate a strong correlation between abnormalities in cerebellar size and the subsequent incidence of cognitive disorders, suggesting that the late-term stage of cerebellar development encompasses a critical developmental time-window for establishing not only the motor but also the non-motor circuitry that is required for complex cerebellar functions and behavior (van der Heijden et al., 2021b; Volpe, 2009; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from clinical observations and supported by citations.

claim: The cerebellum undergoes a series of dynamic developmental changes during the third trimester and early postnatal stages.
source: The cerebellum undergoes a series of dynamic developmental changes during the third trimester and early postnatal stages, a period that corresponds to the first 2 postnatal weeks in mice (Sathyanesan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and is established knowledge in developmental neuroscience.

claim: The third trimester and early postnatal stages in humans correspond to the first 2 postnatal weeks in mice.
source: The cerebellum undergoes a series of dynamic developmental changes during the third trimester and early postnatal stages, a period that corresponds to the first 2 postnatal weeks in mice (Sathyanesan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation establishing the developmental timeline comparison.

claim: The rapid proliferation of granule cell precursors results in a fivefold enlargement of cerebellar size.
source: At the level of gross morphology, the rapid proliferation of granule cell precursors and the integration of granule cells into the cerebellar circuit result in a fivefold enlargement of cerebellar size (Chang et al., 2000), an increase in foliation complexity (Corrales et al., 2006), and the formation of the tri-laminar cerebellar cortex (Miyata et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The integration of granule cells into the cerebellar circuit results in a fivefold enlargement of cerebellar size.
source: At the level of gross morphology, the rapid proliferation of granule cell precursors and the integration of granule cells into the cerebellar circuit result in a fivefold enlargement of cerebellar size (Chang et al., 2000), an increase in foliation complexity (Corrales et al., 2006), and the formation of the tri-laminar cerebellar cortex (Miyata et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The rapid proliferation of granule cell precursors results in an increase in foliation complexity.
source: At the level of gross morphology, the rapid proliferation of granule cell precursors and the integration of granule cells into the cerebellar circuit result in a fivefold enlargement of cerebellar size (Chang et al., 2000), an increase in foliation complexity (Corrales et al., 2006), and the formation of the tri-laminar cerebellar cortex (Miyata et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The rapid proliferation of granule cell precursors results in the formation of the tri-laminar cerebellar cortex.
source: At the level of gross morphology, the rapid proliferation of granule cell precursors and the integration of granule cells into the cerebellar circuit result in a fivefold enlargement of cerebellar size (Chang et al., 2000), an increase in foliation complexity (Corrales et al., 2006), and the formation of the tri-laminar cerebellar cortex (Miyata et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The differentiation and arrival of mature granule cells into the circuit modifies the laminar localization of cerebellar afferents that project to Purkinje cells.
source: At the cellular level, the differentiation and arrival of mature granule cells into the circuit modifies the laminar localization and synaptic specification of cerebellar afferents that project to Purkinje cells (van der Heijden and Sillitoe, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The differentiation and arrival of mature granule cells into the circuit modifies the synaptic specification of cerebellar afferents that project to Purkinje cells.
source: At the cellular level, the differentiation and arrival of mature granule cells into the circuit modifies the laminar localization and synaptic specification of cerebellar afferents that project to Purkinje cells (van der Heijden and Sillitoe, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Perturbations to the cerebellum during the dynamic developmental period may lead to cognitive, social, and motor deficits.
source: Despite an extensive literature describing the temporal anatomical changes in the cerebellum and studies postulating that perturbations to the cerebellum during this dynamic period may lead to cognitive, social, and motor deficits (Volpe, 2009; Wang et al., 2014), there is still relatively little known about how the anatomical aspects of cerebellar development correspond to its functional maturation programs that establish animal behavior.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Preterm birth in pigs results in decreased granule cell numbers.
source: Previous studies show that preterm birth in pigs, as well as postnatal hemorrhage and hypoxia (which mimics cerebellar hemorrhage) in mice, result in decreased granule cell numbers (Iskusnykh et al., 2018; Yoo et al., 2014) and abnormal motor control (Sathyanesan et al., 2018; Yoo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Postnatal hemorrhage in mice results in decreased granule cell numbers.
source: Previous studies show that preterm birth in pigs, as well as postnatal hemorrhage and hypoxia (which mimics cerebellar hemorrhage) in mice, result in decreased granule cell numbers (Iskusnykh et al., 2018; Yoo et al., 2014) and abnormal motor control (Sathyanesan et al., 2018; Yoo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Postnatal hypoxia in mice results in decreased granule cell numbers.
source: Previous studies show that preterm birth in pigs, as well as postnatal hemorrhage and hypoxia (which mimics cerebellar hemorrhage) in mice, result in decreased granule cell numbers (Iskusnykh et al., 2018; Yoo et al., 2014) and abnormal motor control (Sathyanesan et al., 2018; Yoo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Preterm birth in pigs results in abnormal motor control.
source: Previous studies show that preterm birth in pigs, as well as postnatal hemorrhage and hypoxia (which mimics cerebellar hemorrhage) in mice, result in decreased granule cell numbers (Iskusnykh et al., 2018; Yoo et al., 2014) and abnormal motor control (Sathyanesan et al., 2018; Yoo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Postnatal hemorrhage in mice results in abnormal motor control.
source: Previous studies show that preterm birth in pigs, as well as postnatal hemorrhage and hypoxia (which mimics cerebellar hemorrhage) in mice, result in decreased granule cell numbers (Iskusnykh et al., 2018; Yoo et al., 2014) and abnormal motor control (Sathyanesan et al., 2018; Yoo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Postnatal hypoxia causes impairments in the spontaneous firing properties of Purkinje cells in mice.
source: Importantly, postnatal hypoxia causes impairments in the spontaneous firing properties of Purkinje cells in mice (Sathyanesan et al., 2018), and impaired Purkinje cell firing properties are also observed in prematurely born baboons (Barron and Kim, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Impaired Purkinje cell firing properties are observed in prematurely born baboons.
source: Importantly, postnatal hypoxia causes impairments in the spontaneous firing properties of Purkinje cells in mice (Sathyanesan et al., 2018), and impaired Purkinje cell firing properties are also observed in prematurely born baboons (Barron and Kim, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Each Purkinje cell may integrate inputs from up to two hundred fifty thousand excitatory granule cell synapses.
source: It is not surprising that decreasing the number of granule cells results in abnormal Purkinje cell function, since each Purkinje cell may integrate inputs from up to two hundred fifty thousand excitatory granule cell synapses (Huang et al., 2014; Napper and Harvey, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Genetic silencing of granule cells causes only modest alterations to the baseline firing properties of Purkinje cells.
source: Nevertheless, genetic silencing of granule cells causes only modest alterations to the baseline firing properties of Purkinje cells (Galliano et al., 2013), perhaps because the predominant Purkinje cell action potential, called the simple spike, is spontaneously generated by the Purkinje cells (Raman and Bean, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The predominant Purkinje cell action potential, called the simple spike, is spontaneously generated by the Purkinje cells.
source: Nevertheless, genetic silencing of granule cells causes only modest alterations to the baseline firing properties of Purkinje cells (Galliano et al., 2013), perhaps because the predominant Purkinje cell action potential, called the simple spike, is spontaneously generated by the Purkinje cells (Raman and Bean, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Gross motor control is not affected in mice with impaired granule cell signaling.
source: In line with this hypothesis, gross motor control is not affected in mice with impaired granule cell signaling, although they do have impaired motor learning (Galliano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Mice with impaired granule cell signaling have impaired motor learning.
source: In line with this hypothesis, gross motor control is not affected in mice with impaired granule cell signaling, although they do have impaired motor learning (Galliano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Some mouse models that lack the majority of granule cells have severe motor defects.
source: In contrast, some mouse models that lack the majority of granule cells (agranular mice) have such severe motor defects that these mice are named after their phenotype; for example scrambler, weaver, reeler, and staggerer (Bolivar et al., 1996; Falconer, 1951; Heuzé et al., 1997; Le Marec et al., 1997; Sheldon et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies describing these mouse models.

claim: Atoh1 is necessary for the development of excitatory cerebellar neurons.
source: Atoh1 is necessary for the development of excitatory cerebellar neurons (Ben-Arie et al., 1997; Rose et al., 2009) and is not expressed in the inhibitory Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Atoh1 is not expressed in the inhibitory Purkinje cells.
source: Atoh1 is necessary for the development of excitatory cerebellar neurons (Ben-Arie et al., 1997; Rose et al., 2009) and is not expressed in the inhibitory Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Atoh1 expression patterns.

claim: En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice succumb at around weaning age (P21).
source: We previously showed that these En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice are informative for assessing the period of dynamic cerebellar development (P7-P14) but the animals succumb at around weaning age (P21), likely due to a combination of impaired motor coordination and breathing abnormalities (van der Heijden and Zoghbi, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice likely succumb due to a combination of impaired motor coordination and breathing abnormalities.
source: We previously showed that these En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice are informative for assessing the period of dynamic cerebellar development (P7-P14) but the animals succumb at around weaning age (P21), likely due to a combination of impaired motor coordination and breathing abnormalities (van der Heijden and Zoghbi, 2018).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Cerebellar size rapidly expands between P7 and P14 in control mice.
source: We found that cerebellar size rapidly expands between P7 and P14 in control mice (Figure 1D, cerebellum is pseudo-colored in red) but that no such size-expansion occurs in the En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: No cerebellar size-expansion occurs in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice between P7 and P14.
source: We found that cerebellar size rapidly expands between P7 and P14 in control mice (Figure 1D, cerebellum is pseudo-colored in red) but that no such size-expansion occurs in the En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The size of the cerebellum in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice is markedly smaller at both P7 and P14 compared to controls.
source: When we overlay the outlines of the cerebellum, we furthermore observe that the size of the cerebellum in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice is markedly smaller at both P7 and P14 compared to that of similar aged controls (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: P7 and P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- cerebella lack a densely packed granule cell layer.
source: In sagittal tissue sections cut through the hindbrain and then stained with cresyl violet to visualize cell nuclei, we also observe that P7 and P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- cerebella lack a densely packed granule cell layer, that En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- cerebella do not form cerebellar lobules, and that there is no substantial increase in cerebellar size that takes place during the second postnatal week, which are morphological milestones typically observed in control mice (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1G-I.

claim: En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- cerebella do not form cerebellar lobules.
source: In sagittal tissue sections cut through the hindbrain and then stained with cresyl violet to visualize cell nuclei, we also observe that P7 and P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- cerebella lack a densely packed granule cell layer, that En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- cerebella do not form cerebellar lobules, and that there is no substantial increase in cerebellar size that takes place during the second postnatal week, which are morphological milestones typically observed in control mice (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1G-I.

claim: At P14, sagittal cerebellar tissue sections from En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice measure just 11.3% (±1%) the size of paired control tissue sections.
source: At P14, sagittal cerebellar tissue sections from En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice measure just 11.3% (±1%, n=12 sets) the size of paired control tissue sections and in addition, coronal-cut cerebellar tissue sections from En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice measure just 20.2% (±3%, n=6 sets) the size of paired control tissue sections.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: At P14, coronal-cut cerebellar tissue sections from En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice measure just 20.2% (±3%) the size of paired control tissue sections.
source: At P14, sagittal cerebellar tissue sections from En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice measure just 11.3% (±1%, n=12 sets) the size of paired control tissue sections and in addition, coronal-cut cerebellar tissue sections from En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice measure just 20.2% (±3%, n=6 sets) the size of paired control tissue sections.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study.

claim: The deletion of Atoh1 from the En1 domain did not result in gross morphological abnormalities in brain regions other than the cerebellum.
source: Moreover, as expected based on the expression patterns of the two genes we used in our manipulation, the deletion of Atoh1 from just the En1 domain did not result in any gross morphological abnormalities in brain regions other than the cerebellum, including the olfactory bulb, hippocampus, striatum, thalamus, pons, vestibular nuclei, inferior olive, and neocortex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of Atoh1 prevents granule cells from reaching differentiation.
source: We show that deletion of Atoh1 prevents granule cells from reaching differentiation by staining for GABARα6, which marks mature granule cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1–2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There is an approximate thousand-fold reduction in the total number of En1;Atoh1 lineage neurons in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutant mice.
source: We therefore estimate an approximate 103 (thousand)-fold reduction in the total number of En1;Atoh1 lineage neurons in our mutant mice, or less than 1% of the En1;Atoh1 lineage neurons escape the genetic manipulation.
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate based on cell counting data.

claim: Less than 1% of the En1;Atoh1 lineage neurons escape the genetic manipulation in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice.
source: We therefore estimate an approximate 103 (thousand)-fold reduction in the total number of En1;Atoh1 lineage neurons in our mutant mice, or less than 1% of the En1;Atoh1 lineage neurons escape the genetic manipulation.
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate based on cell counting data.

claim: En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice have a reduced pool of excitatory unipolar brush cells.
source: Consistent with the substantially reduced number of En1;Atoh1 lineage neurons in the conditional knockout mice, we observe that En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- conditional knockout mice have a reduced pool of excitatory unipolar brush cells, which also derive from the En1;Atoh1 lineage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1–4A), compared to the density of unipolar brush cells that are localized to lobule IX and X in control mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: There is an approximately eight-fold reduction in the number of unipolar brush cells in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice.
source: When we counted the number Tbr2+unipolar brush cells in control and conditional knockout mice, we found an approximately eight-fold reduction in the number of unipolar brush cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C–E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C-E.

claim: There is an approximate fivefold reduction in the number of excitatory cerebellar nuclei neurons in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice.
source: We also counted the number of excitatory cerebellar nuclei neurons, that derive from the En1;Atoh1 lineage (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B) and found an approximate fivefold reduction in their number (Figure 1—figure supplement 4F–H).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the study shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4F-H.

claim: The representation of different classes of inhibitory neurons remains robust in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice.
source: In line with our conditional knockout that targets neurons in the excitatory lineage, we further found that the representation of different classes of inhibitory neurons, including molecular layer interneurons, basket cells, and Golgi cells, remains robust and clearly detected by cell-type-specific markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E-H.

claim: Purkinje cells differentiate into distinct molecular subtypes shortly after birth.
source: While Purkinje cells differentiate into distinct molecular subtypes shortly after birth (Wassef et al., 1990), they initially group together into cellular clusters and only form the more precise and sharply delineated longitudinal zones as the cerebellum greatly expands in size and volume (Dastjerdi et al., 2012; Larouche and Hawkes, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Purkinje cells initially group together into cellular clusters and only form the more precise and sharply delineated longitudinal zones as the cerebellum greatly expands in size and volume.
source: While Purkinje cells differentiate into distinct molecular subtypes shortly after birth (Wassef et al., 1990), they initially group together into cellular clusters and only form the more precise and sharply delineated longitudinal zones as the cerebellum greatly expands in size and volume (Dastjerdi et al., 2012; Larouche and Hawkes, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: At P14, ZebrinII+ and PLCβ4+ expressing Purkinje cells in control mice are organized in alternating zones.
source: As expected, at P14, ZebrinII+ and PLCβ4+ expressing Purkinje cells in control mice are organized in alternating zones (Figure 2A–G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A-G.

claim: ZebrinII+ and PLCβ4+ expression patterns in the En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- cerebellum are organized into a series of clusters rather than sharp zones.
source: In contrast, ZebrinII+ and PLCβ4+ expression patterns in the En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- cerebellum are organized into a series of clusters rather than sharp zones.
evidence: This is a finding from the study comparing mutant to control patterns.

claim: The overall pattern of clusters in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants resembles the architecture that is typically observed in normal neonates.
source: The overall pattern of clusters in the mutants resembles the architecture that is typically observed in normal neonates (Figure 2H–N; Fujita et al., 2012; Sugihara and Fujita, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2H-N and citations to previous studies.

claim: Some Purkinje cells over-migrate beyond the boundaries of the cerebellum and into the inferior colliculus in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice.
source: Some Purkinje cells, here marked with PLCβ4+, over-migrate beyond the boundaries of the cerebellum and into the inferior colliculus that is immediately adjacent (arrowheads Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Co-expression of ZebrinII+ and PLCβ4+ occurs in the same clusters of cells in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice.
source: We also observed co-expression of ZebrinII+ and PLCβ4+ in the same clusters of cells in the En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice (arrowheads Figure 2M–N).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2M-N.

claim: Postnatal ZebrinII+ expression sweeps over the whole cerebellum becoming expressed in all Purkinje cells by around P10, before it segments into zones by ~P15.
source: In normal mice, postnatal ZebrinII+ expression sweeps over the whole cerebellum becoming expressed in all Purkinje cells by around P10, before it segments into zones by ~P15 (Tano et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Spinal cord mossy fibers send their projections to the granular layer below ZebrinII- zones.
source: For example, spinal cord mossy fibers send their projections to the granular layer below ZebrinII- zones (Sillitoe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: During development, spinal cord mossy fiber projections directly target Purkinje cells.
source: During development, these projections directly target Purkinje cells (Kalinovsky et al., 2011; Sillitoe, 2016), but with the integration of granule cells into the circuit, mossy fibers displace their synapses onto granule cells (Arsénio Nunes et al., 1988; Pan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: With the integration of granule cells into the circuit, mossy fibers displace their synapses onto granule cells.
source: During development, these projections directly target Purkinje cells (Kalinovsky et al., 2011; Sillitoe, 2016), but with the integration of granule cells into the circuit, mossy fibers displace their synapses onto granule cells (Arsénio Nunes et al., 1988; Pan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In controls, mossy fibers project to the cerebellar cortex in a zonal pattern that reflects the topography of ZebrinII.
source: In controls, mossy fibers project to the cerebellar cortex in a zonal pattern that reflects the topography of ZebrinII (Figure 2O–P; Brochu et al., 1990; Sillitoe and Hawkes, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2O-P and citations to previous studies.

claim: Spinocerebellar mossy fibers project mainly to ZebrinII- domains in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice.
source: As in the controls, we found that spinocerebellar mossy fibers projected mainly to ZebrinII- domains in the En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: In controls, mossy fibers occupy the domains in the granular layer that are located directly below the Purkinje cell zones, whereas in the mutants the mossy fibers remain intermingled within Purkinje cell clusters.
source: However, in controls the mossy fibers occupy the domains in the granular layer that are located directly below the Purkinje cell zones, whereas in the mutants the mossy fibers remain intermingled within Purkinje cell clusters (Figure 2O–Q).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2O-Q.

claim: Excitatory cerebellar neurons are not essential for initiating the zonal topography of mossy fiber projections that arise from the spinal cord.
source: These results confirm that excitatory cerebellar neurons are not essential for initiating the zonal topography of mossy fiber projections that arise from the spinal cord.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Integration of excitatory neurons into the circuit is important for the architectural rearrangement and the refinement of both the Purkinje cells and afferents into zones.
source: However, the organization of mossy fibers into poorly defined clusters in the mutants indicates that integration of excitatory neurons into the circuit is important for the architectural rearrangement and the refinement of both the Purkinje cells and afferents into zones.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Decreasing excitatory input alters Purkinje cell dendrite outgrowth.
source: Previous studies suggest that decreasing excitatory input alters Purkinje cell dendrite outgrowth (Bradley and Berry, 1976; Pan et al., 2009; Park et al., 2019; Takeo et al., 2021), which results in abnormal dendrite morphology in agranular mice (Sotelo and Dusart, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Purkinje cells in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice have stunted and smaller dendritic arbors compared to controls.
source: We found that Purkinje cells in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice had stunted and smaller dendritic arbors compared to the controls (Figure 3A), and unlike in the control cerebella, neighboring Purkinje cells did not orient their arbors in the same direction (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Neighboring Purkinje cells in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice do not orient their arbors in the same direction.
source: We found that Purkinje cells in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice had stunted and smaller dendritic arbors compared to the controls (Figure 3A), and unlike in the control cerebella, neighboring Purkinje cells did not orient their arbors in the same direction (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Purkinje cells in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants are smaller with less bifurcated dendritic branches.
source: Sholl analysis revealed that the Purkinje cells in the mutants were smaller with less bifurcated dendritic branches (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Spine density is significantly lower in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice compared to control mice.
source: Furthermore, spine density was significantly lower in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice compared to the control mice (Figure 3D–E), which is in agreement with previous work showing that dendrite outgrowth is dependent on the formation of excitatory synapses, the majority of which are contributed from granule cell parallel fibers in control animals (Bradley and Berry, 1976; Pan et al., 2009; Park et al., 2019; Takeo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D-E and citations to previous studies.

claim: Dendrite outgrowth is dependent on the formation of excitatory synapses, the majority of which are contributed from granule cell parallel fibers in control animals.
source: Furthermore, spine density was significantly lower in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice compared to the control mice (Figure 3D–E), which is in agreement with previous work showing that dendrite outgrowth is dependent on the formation of excitatory synapses, the majority of which are contributed from granule cell parallel fibers in control animals (Bradley and Berry, 1976; Pan et al., 2009; Park et al., 2019; Takeo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: From P7 to P14, a large population of excitatory (Vglut1+) granule cells integrate into the cerebellar circuit and make direct contacts to Purkinje cells via their parallel fibers in the molecular layer.
source: From P7 to P14, a large population of excitatory (Vglut1+) granule cells integrate into the cerebellar circuit and make direct contacts to Purkinje cells via their parallel fibers in the molecular layer (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar development illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: There is an increase in the density of Vglut1+ synapses in the Purkinje cell layer and molecular layer from P7 to P14 in control mice.
source: We saw an increase in the density of Vglut1+ synapses in the Purkinje cell layer and molecular layer from P7 to P14 in control mice (Figure 4B, top row).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The signal of Vglut1+ synapses in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice does not change between P7 and P14.
source: Indeed, we saw that the signal of Vglut1+ synapses in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice did not change between P7 and P14 (Figure 4B, bottom row) and quantification showed that this signal was significantly lower at both time points in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice compared to age-matched control mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Vglut1+ signal is significantly lower at both P7 and P14 in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice compared to age-matched control mice.
source: Indeed, we saw that the signal of Vglut1+ synapses in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice did not change between P7 and P14 (Figure 4B, bottom row) and quantification showed that this signal was significantly lower at both time points in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice compared to age-matched control mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There is an approximately nine-fold reduction in Vglut1+ signal in the cerebella of En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice.
source: However, the approximately nine-fold reduction in Vglut1+ signal in the cerebella of En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice further confirms that our conditional knockout strategy impairs the integration of granule cells into the cerebellar circuit.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study.

claim: Purkinje cells have a distinct firing profile characterized by spontaneously generated simple spikes and climbing fiber-induced complex spikes.
source: Purkinje cells have a distinct firing profile characterized by spontaneously generated simple spikes and climbing fiber-induced complex spikes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Purkinje cell physiology.

claim: Purkinje cells recorded from P14 control mice have the highest peak firing frequency.
source: Based on the time points we tested, and in line with the highest Vglut1+ density in P14 control mice, Purkinje cells recorded from these mice had the highest peak firing frequency, whereas Purkinje cells in P7 control mice had an overall lower firing rate (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Purkinje cells in P7 control mice have an overall lower firing rate than P14 control mice.
source: Based on the time points we tested, and in line with the highest Vglut1+ density in P14 control mice, Purkinje cells recorded from these mice had the highest peak firing frequency, whereas Purkinje cells in P7 control mice had an overall lower firing rate (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: There is a statistically significant increase in frequency and frequency mode from P7-10 to P11-14 in control mice.
source: We found that there is a statistically significant increase in frequency and frequency mode from P7-10 to P11-14 (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5F-G.

claim: There is a statistically significant increase in CV and pause proportion from P7-12 to P13-14 in control mice.
source: We also found a statistically significant increase in CV and pause proportion from P7-12 to P13-14 (Figure 5J–K).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5J-K.

claim: There is an increase in the rhythmicity index from P7-10 to P11-14 in control mice.
source: In addition, there was an increase in the rhythmicity index from P7-10 to P11-14 (Figure 5N), but no change in the CV2 (Figure 5O).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5N.

claim: There is no change in CV2 between P7-10 and P11-14 in control mice.
source: In addition, there was an increase in the rhythmicity index from P7-10 to P11-14 (Figure 5N), but no change in the CV2 (Figure 5O).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5O.

claim: Spontaneous simple spikes in Purkinje cells recorded in P10 and P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants have a lower frequency and frequency mode than those recorded in Purkinje cells in P11-14 control mice.
source: We found that spontaneous simple spikes in Purkinje cells recorded in P10 and P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants had a lower frequency and frequency mode than those recorded in Purkinje cells in P11-14 control mice (Figure 5D–G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D-G.

claim: The CV and pause proportion are significantly lower in Purkinje cells recorded from P10 and P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants compared to P13-14 control Purkinje cells.
source: We also found that the CV and pause proportion was significantly lower in Purkinje cells recorded from P10 and P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants compared to the P13-14 control Purkinje cells (Figure 5H–K).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5H-K.

claim: Purkinje cells recorded from P10 and P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants have a lower rhythmicity index than P11-14 control Purkinje cells.
source: In addition, we found that Purkinje cells recorded from P10 and P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants had a lower rhythmicity index than the P11-14 control Purkinje cells (Figure 5L–N) and a higher CV2 than all control Purkinje cells (Figure 5O).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5L-N.

claim: Purkinje cells recorded from P10 and P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants have a higher CV2 than all control Purkinje cells.
source: In addition, we found that Purkinje cells recorded from P10 and P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants had a lower rhythmicity index than the P11-14 control Purkinje cells (Figure 5L–N) and a higher CV2 than all control Purkinje cells (Figure 5O).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5O.

claim: Purkinje cell firing patterns in P10 and P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants never differ from each other in any of the six parameters analyzed.
source: Finally, we found that Purkinje cell firing patterns in P10 and P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants never differed from each other in any of the six parameters that we included in our analysis.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Purkinje cells in P10 and P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants have a firing pattern that is highly similar to Purkinje cells in P7-10 control mice.
source: Together, these results suggest that the changes in Purkinje firing patterns that occur between P7-10 and P13-14 in control animals does not occur in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants, and that Purkinje cells in P10 and in P14 in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants have a firing pattern that is highly similar to Purkinje cells in the P7-10 control mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Purkinje cells from both P10 and P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice cluster with young control cells in unbiased cluster analysis.
source: When we retrospectively label the age and genotype of each cell after unbiased clustering, we see that older control cells cluster together (P11-14 in difference shades of green, clustered at the top) and younger control cells cluster together (P7-10 in different shades of purple, cluster at the bottom). Interestingly, Purkinje cells from both P10 and P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice cluster with the young control cells (orange, at the bottom) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Purkinje cells from both P10 and P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice cluster with young (P7-10) control cells in t-SNE analysis.
source: After retrospectively color-coding the data points, we present a pseudo-timeline of the developmental transformation of firing patterns, with Purkinje cells from both P10 and P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice clustered with the young (P7-10) control cells in the bottom right and older (P11-14) control cells on clustered together on the top left (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The P10 and P14 Purkinje cells recorded in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice cluster with the young control cells (P7-10) and do not undergo the functional transformation in firing patterns that Purkinje cells in control mice do.
source: In agreement with our aforementioned findings, we found that the P10 and P14 Purkinje cells recorded in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice cluster with the young control cells (P7-10) and do not undergo the functional transformation in firing patterns that Purkinje cells in control mice do.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cluster analysis data.

claim: Purkinje cells undergo a major developmental transformation in firing patterns between P7-10 and P11-14.
source: Taken together, in a period of dynamic circuit development, Purkinje cells undergo a major developmental transformation in firing patterns between P7-10 and P11-14.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The developmental transformation in Purkinje cell firing patterns does not occur between P10 and P14 in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice.
source: Furthermore, in agreement with the absence of change in gross cerebellar morphology or dynamics in Vglut1+ synapses, this developmental transformation does not occur between P10 and P14 in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: During early postnatal development, multiple climbing fibers contact one Purkinje cell.
source: Interestingly, during early postnatal development, multiple climbing fibers contact one Purkinje cell, but in a parallel-fiber/granule cell-dependent process, the additional climbing fibers are pruned away during the second and third weeks of life (Crepel and Delhaye-Bouchaud, 1979; Hashimoto et al., 2009; Kano and Hashimoto, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In a parallel-fiber/granule cell-dependent process, additional climbing fibers are pruned away during the second and third weeks of life.
source: Interestingly, during early postnatal development, multiple climbing fibers contact one Purkinje cell, but in a parallel-fiber/granule cell-dependent process, the additional climbing fibers are pruned away during the second and third weeks of life (Crepel and Delhaye-Bouchaud, 1979; Hashimoto et al., 2009; Kano and Hashimoto, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Immature Vglut2+/climbing fiber synapses are located around the Purkinje cell body in controls.
source: Immature Vglut2+/climbing fiber synapses are located around the Purkinje cell body in controls, but at around P9 only the 'winner' among these synapses translocates to the Purkinje cell dendrites in the molecular layer (Kano et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: At around P9, only the 'winner' climbing fiber synapse translocates to the Purkinje cell dendrites in the molecular layer.
source: Immature Vglut2+/climbing fiber synapses are located around the Purkinje cell body in controls, but at around P9 only the 'winner' among these synapses translocates to the Purkinje cell dendrites in the molecular layer (Kano et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: There is a decrease in the density of Vglut2+ synapses in P14 control cerebella compared to P7.
source: Indeed, we observed a decrease in the density of Vglut2+ synapses in P14 control cerebella compared to P7, likely due to a combined reduction in Vglut2+ expression in granule cells, displacement of mossy fibers to granule cells, and pruning of climbing fibers (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: There is a high density of Vglut2+ synapses in the cerebella of En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice at both P7 and P14.
source: At both timepoints, however, we observed a high density of Vglut2+ synapses in the cerebella of En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: The number of soma-associated Vglut2+ contacts on Purkinje cells decreases between P7 and P14 in control mice.
source: As expected, the number of soma-associated Vglut2+ contacts on Purkinje cells decreased between P7 and P14 in control mice, whereas all Purkinje cell somata in the En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice remained enriched with Vglut2+ synapses (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: All Purkinje cell somata in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice remain enriched with Vglut2+ synapses at P7 and P14.
source: As expected, the number of soma-associated Vglut2+ contacts on Purkinje cells decreased between P7 and P14 in control mice, whereas all Purkinje cell somata in the En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice remained enriched with Vglut2+ synapses (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: En1;Atoh1 lineage excitatory cerebellar neurons are necessary for shaping the regional localization and cellular targeting of immature mossy fibers and climbing fibers that project to Purkinje cells.
source: These data show that the En1;Atoh1 lineage, excitatory cerebellar neurons are necessary for shaping the regional localization and cellular targeting of immature mossy fibers and climbing fibers that project to the Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Purkinje cells in P14 control mice fire classical complex spikes, which are defined by a large sodium spike followed by a train of three to five smaller spikelets.
source: Purkinje cells in P14 control mice fired classical complex spikes, which are defined by a large sodium spike followed by a train of three to five smaller spikelets (Davie et al., 2008; Zagha et al., 2008; Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8B and citations to previous studies.

claim: Purkinje cells in P7 control mice fire 'doublets', which are characterized by an initial simple spike-like action potential, followed by a smaller action potential that occurs within 20 ms.
source: In contrast, Purkinje cells in P7 control mice fire 'doublets', which are characterized by an initial simple spike-like action potential, followed by a smaller action potential that occurs within 20 ms (a similar profile of doublets was previously reported in neonatal rats [Puro and Woodward, 1977; Sokoloff et al., 2015, Figure 8A]).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8A and citations to previous studies.

claim: Purkinje cells in P10 and P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice predominantly fire doublets instead of true complex spikes.
source: Similar to Purkinje cells in P7 control mice, the Purkinje cells in P10 and P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice also predominantly fired doublets instead of true complex spikes, suggesting that the extrinsically-induced action potentials in Purkinje cells are maintained in an immature state just like the firing patterns of spontaneous simple spikes (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Purkinje cells recorded in P11-14 control mice have a statistically significant higher frequency of complex spikes than Purkinje cells recorded from P7 to P10 control mice and P10 to P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants.
source: Specifically, we found that Purkinje cells recorded in P11-14 control mice had a statistically significant higher frequency of complex spikes than Purkinje cells recorded from P7 to P10 control mice and P10 to P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The frequency of doublets is significantly higher in Purkinje cells recorded from P10 to P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants than in Purkinje cells in control animals of all ages.
source: Conversely, the frequency of doublets was significantly higher in Purkinje cells recorded from P10 to P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants than in Purkinje cells in control animals of all ages (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: The number of all combined complex spikes is higher in Purkinje cells recorded from P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants than in Purkinje cells recorded in P7-8, P9-10, and P13-14 control animals.
source: In addition, the number of all combined complex spikes was higher in Purkinje cells recorded from in P14 En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutants than that observed in Purkinje cells recorded in P7-8, P9-10, and P13-14 control animals (Figure 8H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8H.

claim: Purkinje cells in mutant mice do not acquire a similar maturation in overall complex spike shape that control Purkinje cells do.
source: Together, these results indicate that the Purkinje cells in the mutant mice do not acquire a similar maturation in overall complex spike shape that the control Purkinje cells do and they have a high number of immature-like doublets, which may indicate an altered pruning process of immature climbing fibers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Purkinje cells in mutant mice have a high number of immature-like doublets, which may indicate an altered pruning process of immature climbing fibers.
source: Together, these results indicate that the Purkinje cells in the mutant mice do not acquire a similar maturation in overall complex spike shape that the control Purkinje cells do and they have a high number of immature-like doublets, which may indicate an altered pruning process of immature climbing fibers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with speculative interpretation.

claim: Purkinje cells send projections to the cerebellar nuclei and some direct projections to the vestibular nuclei.
source: Purkinje cells send projections to the cerebellar nuclei, which consists of both excitatory and inhibitory neurons, as well as some direct projections to the vestibular nuclei (Sillitoe and Joyner, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Cerebellar circuits are important for motor coordination and balance as well as social behaviors including ultrasonic vocalization (USV) in neonatal pups.
source: These circuits are important for motor coordination and balance as well as social behaviors including ultrasonic vocalization (USV) in neonatal pups (Fujita et al., 2008; Lalonde and Strazielle, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: At P14, control mice explore an open arena with smooth intentional motions, whereas En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice often fall on their backs.
source: At P14, control mice explore an open arena with smooth intentional motions, whereas En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice often fall on their backs.
evidence: This is an observation from behavioral experiments.

claim: En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice perform poorly compared to control littermates during the righting reflex.
source: We found that En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice perform poorly compared to control littermates during the righting reflex. They were significantly slower in returning onto four paws when compared to Atoh1fl/+ control mice at P8 and P10, and they were slower than heterozygous En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/+mice only at P10 (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Call time in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice is shorter than those observed in control littermates.
source: We found that call time in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice was shorter than those observed in control littermates and that En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice called less frequently than Atoh1fl/+ mice (Figure 9C–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9C-E.

claim: En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice call less frequently than Atoh1fl/+ mice.
source: We found that call time in En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice was shorter than those observed in control littermates and that En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice called less frequently than Atoh1fl/+ mice (Figure 9C–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9C-E.

claim: En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutant mice travel slower than Atoh1fl/- control mice.
source: However, En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutant mice traveled slower than Atoh1fl/- control mice and the En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/+ mice made more isolated movements during their trajectory compared to all their littermate controls (Figure 9F–H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9F-H.

claim: En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/+ mice make more isolated movements during their trajectory compared to all their littermate controls.
source: However, En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mutant mice traveled slower than Atoh1fl/- control mice and the En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/+ mice made more isolated movements during their trajectory compared to all their littermate controls (Figure 9F–H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9F-H.

claim: En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice have a higher power tremor in the 12–16 Hz frequency range.
source: We found that En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice had a higher power tremor in the 12–16 Hz frequency range (Figure 9J).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9J.

claim: The mutant mice have a higher peak tremor power compared to all control littermates.
source: The mutant mice also had a higher peak tremor power compared to all control littermates (Figure 9K).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9K.

claim: The lack of rRL-derived excitatory cerebellar neurons in developing En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice leads to multiple abnormal cerebellar-dependent behaviors that are observed in the first 2 weeks of postnatal life.
source: Together, we uncovered that the lack of rRL-derived excitatory cerebellar neurons in developing En1Cre/+;Atoh1fl/- mice leads to multiple abnormal cerebellar-dependent behaviors that are observed in the first 2 weeks of postnatal life.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral experiments.

claim: Loss of granule cell neurogenesis stalls the anatomical and functional maturation of postnatal Purkinje cells.
source: Using this model with circuit-wide loss of granule cell neurogenesis, we uncovered how these late-born cells influence the functional development of their downstream synaptic partners, the Purkinje cells. We find that granule cell elimination stalls the anatomical and functional maturation of postnatal Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: Granule cell neurogenesis is impaired in premature infants with cerebellar hemorrhages.
source: In humans, granule cell neurogenesis is impaired in premature infants with cerebellar hemorrhages, which is expected as proliferating granule cell precursors are highly vulnerable to the hemorrhage, likely because of their high metabolic demand (Dobbing, 1974; Gano and Barkovich, 2019; Hortensius et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Proliferating granule cell precursors are highly vulnerable to hemorrhage, likely because of their high metabolic demand.
source: In humans, granule cell neurogenesis is impaired in premature infants with cerebellar hemorrhages, which is expected as proliferating granule cell precursors are highly vulnerable to the hemorrhage, likely because of their high metabolic demand (Dobbing, 1974; Gano and Barkovich, 2019; Hortensius et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Loss of just a few granule cell precursors has exponential effects on the number of granule cells that integrate into the cerebellar circuit.
source: Moreover, even a localized lesion that occurs during early cerebellar genesis can have major repercussions; loss of just a few precursors has exponential effects on the number of granule cells that integrate into the cerebellar circuit (Corrales et al., 2004; Corrales et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The initial communication between Purkinje cells and granule cells sets the efficiency of Purkinje cell function and the establishment of Purkinje cell spike properties through structural as well as synaptic signals.
source: Based on our data, we argue that the initial communication between Purkinje cells and granule cells sets the efficiency of Purkinje cell function and the establishment of Purkinje cell spike properties through structural as well as synaptic signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Insults to granule cell proliferation and an obstruction of granule cell neurogenesis may have different, and perhaps more severe effects on downstream Purkinje cell function, compared to lesions of mature granule cells.
source: Thus, insults to granule cell proliferation and an obstruction of granule cell neurogenesis may have different, and perhaps more severe effects on downstream Purkinje cell function, compared to lesions of mature granule cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing different experimental approaches.
